body:
So what you say is it only stops reading once the all data is read from the socket ?

Am 15.05.2013 um 17:25 schrieb Olivier SOTIN notifications@github.com:

> I don't be able to make this feature works correcly.
> 
> I've got a simple pipeline with a single handler "MyHandler" which reads bytes from the inboundbuffer and writes them into a queue. This queue is read by another thread.
> When this queue is full, it does'nt block, so my IO thread can return and exit MyHandler.inboundBufferUpdated() method.
> 
> The way autoread=false works (or what I understood), I should not have new inboundBufferUpdated() call as long as ctx.read() is not called.
> However, inboundBufferUpdated() method is called as long as IO thread has bytes to read from channel socket. When socket becomes "empty", read is suspended, but
> if socket contains bytes, there's no option to stop the "stream".
> 
> Here is my analysis (and so possible issue):
> In AbstractNioByteChannel.NioByteUnsafe::read() method, if pipeline.fireInboundBufferUpdated() is called from "case2" (when inbound buffer has reached its max capacity) there's no way to exit loop even if autoread=false
> 
> —
> Reply to this email directly or view it on GitHub.

@normanmaurer 

Yes,

In **"AbstractNioByteChannel.NioByteUnsafe::read()"** method, we have a loop for(;;) from which we cannot exit as long as socket is not empty.
We first read from socket and then enter a switch:

**case 0**: all data has been read from socket -> exit loop and call **inboundBufferUpdated()**. After **inboundBufferUpdated()** call -> exit read() method, so _"autoread=false"_ mode works correctly in this case.

**case 1**: not all data has been read, buffer has been expanded, so we loop again to read more data. ok

**case 2**: not all data has been read, buffer is full, comment is _"Let the inbound handler drain the buffer and continue reading"_. 
But, in this case, **fireInboundBufferUpdated()** is always called, even if it was already called since last ctx.read() call (in _"autoread=false"_ mode)
After what, we are still in loop, if socket contains enough data to fill inboundBuffer, case 2 is reached again and **fireInboundBufferUpdated()** is called again, and so on

Ok got it... Let me check

@normanmaurer @trustin 

I've got another _"issue"_ with _"autoread=false"_ feature.

Use case:
Only one handler in the pipeline called "MyHandler".
In **myHandler.inboundBufferUpdated()**, some bytes from inbound buffer are consumed. Netty allows us to exit this method even if inboundbuffer contains data.
When method exits, no more call to **inboundBufferUpdated()** as long as **ctx.read()** is not called. Ok. 

But if, at this point of time, channel socket does'nt contains more data and inboundBuffer contains remaining bytes, a call to **ctx.read()** does nothing because nothing new to read, so no event from selector and so inboundBuffer is not updated and so **myHandler.inboundBufferUpdated()** is never called.
If myHandler want to drain remaining bytes, a call to ctx.pipeline().firstContext().fireInboundBufferUpdated() can help.
But from a "myHandler view", it's hard to now if we need to call ctx.read() (because socket potentially contains data) or **fireInboundBufferUpdated()** to drain remaining bytes.

This is a bug indeed.  Thanks for the detailed explanation.

@trustin @Totin actually I'm not sure if the second one is really a bug.... I would tempted to say that you should intercept ChannelOperationHandler.read(...) to drain the buffer in this case.

The first issue is fixed

@normanmaurer @trustin Thanks for the bug fix, It works fine now.

For the second one, I'm ok to say that it's no really a bug as it works. 
However, from my point of view, API must be easy to use. 

Today, if I want to code a handler that process all bytes from a socket with _autoread(false)_, I always need to care about which "resume function" should I use. 
At the end of **myHandler.inboundBufferUpdated()** method, I test if **"inboundBuffer.readableBytes() > 0"**. If yes, I set the "resume function" to **"ctx.pipeline().firstContext().fireInboundBufferUpdated()"**, otherwise I set it to **"ctx.read()"**.

Intercepting **ChannelOperationHandler.read(...)** could be a better way, but if we need to always do this, it must be done as default... It's still my point of view ;)

@Totin I just wonder how calling inboundBufferUpdated() will help you if you have two handlers in the pipeline and the first just "surpress" the call to ctx.fireInboundBufferUpdated() as it has not enough data to generate another frame. In this situation the second handler may have enough bytes for you to process but you will not get notified.

@normanmaurer In such a case, he could call `ctx.handler().inboundBufferUpdated()` instead of `ctx.pipeline().firstContext().fireInboundBufferUpdated()`.  His opinion is, to my understanding, that it will be more convenient if Netty just triggers `inboundBufferUpdated()` on the `ChannelHandlerContext` which `read()` operation runs against when the its inbound buffer is not empty.

However, the proposed behavior is redundant and only useful for a certain use case.  If it is triggered when an inbound buffer is not updated (no data was appended at all in this case yet), it's not an `inboundBufferUpdated()` anymore.
